tool.name: Ansible
tool.tagline: Agentless automation for configuring servers and deploying software over SSH
tool.description: Ansible automates server configuration, application deployment and routine operations by running idempotent tasks, written as YAML playbooks, on many machines over SSH with nothing to install on them. It is widely used to configure VMs and bare metal, often after Terraform has created them, and to manage network devices.

glossary.def: The computer you run Ansible from, usually your laptop or a build server. It logs in to the other machines and tells them what to do.
A server or device that Ansible looks after. Nothing extra has to run on it; Ansible reaches it over SSH when it has work to do.
Needing no helper program installed and running on each managed machine: Ansible just logs in over SSH when it has work to do.
In Ansible: a small ready-made program that does one job on a host, such as installing a package or copying a file, and reports whether it changed anything.
Ansible's list of the machines it manages, sorted into groups, with the details it needs to reach each one.
The expression that picks which inventory hosts a run acts on, such as web (one group), web:&prod (hosts in both groups) or all:!staging (all but staging).
One Ansible module run on a set of hosts straight from the terminal, without writing a playbook.
A practice run that reports what would change without actually changing anything.
A bundle of Ansible modules, roles and add-ons published together under a two-part name like community.general, installed from Ansible Galaxy.
The full name of an Ansible module, with its collection in front: ansible.builtin.copy instead of just copy.
A YAML file of steps for Ansible: which hosts to work on and which tasks to run on them, in order. You run it with ansible-playbook.
The fill-in-the-blanks language Ansible uses for variables and templates: {{ name }} prints a value, and {% if %} and {% for %} add choices and repeats.
A piece of information Ansible collects about each host when a play starts, such as its operating system, IP addresses or memory, usable as a variable.
Variables given on the ansible-playbook command with -e key=value. They beat every other place the same variable is set.
An Ansible task that runs only when a task that changed something notifies it, typically to reload a service. It runs once, at the end of the play.
Running a task as a more powerful user, usually root via sudo. In Ansible you turn it on with become: true.
A function written after a | in Jinja2 that transforms a value, like {{ name | upper }} or {{ list | join(', ') }}.
A folder with a fixed layout that packs the tasks, handlers, templates and default settings for one job, so it can be reused across playbooks.
Ansible's built-in tool for encrypting secrets such as passwords, so they can be stored with your playbooks and are decrypted only while Ansible runs.
Updating a group of servers a few at a time, so most keep working and a bad update can be stopped before it reaches all of them.
Ansible's dry-run mode (--check): every module reports what it would change without changing anything.
A checker that reads Ansible playbooks and roles without running them and flags mistakes and bad habits.
A testing tool for Ansible roles: it creates throwaway test machines, applies the role twice, runs checks, then deletes the machines.
The public website where people share Ansible collections and roles; the ansible-galaxy command installs from it.
A container image holding ansible-core, chosen collections and the libraries they need, so every Ansible run uses exactly the same setup.
In Ansible, forks is how many hosts work on a task at the same time, each through its own worker process. The default is 5.
An Ansible speed-up that sends each module through the already-open SSH connection instead of first copying it to the host as a file.
Saving the facts Ansible gathered about hosts between runs, so it doesn't have to collect them from every host again.
A plugin that builds Ansible's host list at run time by asking an outside source, such as a cloud provider, which machines exist right now.
Code on the control node that runs for every task before its module. Usually it just sends the module off; for template or copy it does work locally first.
The part of Ansible that carries code and data to a host: ssh by default, or local, winrm for Windows and others.
The single self-unpacking file Ansible builds from a Python module and its helper code, then sends to the host and runs there.
The ansible-core 2.19+ templating system in which every value remembers where it came from and whether it can be trusted, for stricter rules and precise error messages.

concepts.name: What Ansible is: agentless and idempotent
concepts.summary: Ansible logs in to your servers over SSH, runs small modules that bring each one to the state you described, and reports what changed.
concepts.why: How Ansible works (it pushes changes over SSH, and running it again is safe) explains how everything else in it behaves.
concepts.body:
Imagine you look after ten servers. Each needs the same software installed, the same configuration files and the same user accounts. You could SSH into each one and type the commands ten times: slow, boring and easy to get wrong. **Ansible** does it for you. You write down once what every server should look like, and Ansible logs in to each one over SSH and makes it so.

The computer you run Ansible from, usually your own laptop, is the **control node**. The servers it looks after are **managed nodes**. Linux managed nodes need only SSH and Python (a popular language for writing programs, which almost every Linux distribution already includes).

Nothing else has to be installed on the managed nodes. Many older tools need an **agent**: a helper program that runs on every server all the time, waiting for instructions. Ansible needs no such helper, which is why it's called **agentless**: it simply logs in when it has work to do.

You describe what you want as a list of **tasks**. Each task calls a **module**: a small ready-made program that does one job, such as installing a package, copying a file or starting a service. Ansible sends the module to the server, runs it there, and gets back a short report saying whether anything **changed**.

Modules check before they act. Asked for "the package nginx (a program that serves websites) is installed", the module installs it the first time; on later runs it sees nginx is already there and does nothing. Something that gives the same result whether you do it once or many times is **idempotent**, like pressing a lift button again: the lift is already coming. So running Ansible twice is safe, and the second run should report `changed=0`.

You'll hear Ansible compared with other tools:

- **Terraform** creates the servers themselves at a **cloud provider** (a company that rents out servers, such as AWS); Ansible then sets up what runs on them. Many teams use both.
- **Puppet** and **Chef** put an agent on every server that regularly fetches its settings; Ansible pushes changes when you run it.

You install Ansible only on the control node, for example with `pipx install ansible` (pipx is an installer for programs written in Python).
concepts.code:
# install Ansible on the control node (your laptop)
pipx install --include-deps ansible
ansible --version | head -1
# ansible [core 2.21.x]

# run the ping module against this computer itself
ansible localhost -m ansible.builtin.ping
# localhost | SUCCESS => {"changed": false, "ping": "pong"}

# ask the file module for a directory: the first run creates it...
ansible localhost -m ansible.builtin.file -a "path=/tmp/demo state=directory"
# localhost | CHANGED => {... "changed": true ...}
# ...the second run finds it already there and changes nothing (idempotent)
ansible localhost -m ansible.builtin.file -a "path=/tmp/demo state=directory"
# localhost | SUCCESS => {... "changed": false ...}
takeaways: Agentless: managed nodes need only SSH and Python
Tasks call modules, which report changed or ok
Idempotent: a second run changes nothing
pitfalls: Making a task run a raw shell command that acts every time, so every run reports a change and repeating it isn't safe.

quiz.q: You run the same Ansible tasks twice in a row on a server nobody else touched. What should the second run report?
options: The same changed count as the first
An error because things already exist
quiz.explain: Idempotent modules see the server is already in the requested state and change nothing.

concepts.name: Inventory: hosts and groups
concepts.summary: List the servers Ansible manages in an inventory file, sort them into groups, and say how to reach each one.
concepts.why: Every Ansible run picks its servers from an inventory; groups are how you aim work at the right machines.
concepts.body:
Before Ansible can do anything, it needs a list of the servers it looks after and how to reach each one. That list is the **inventory**, usually a file in your project folder.

Ansible's files are mostly written in **YAML**, a plain-text format designed to be easy for people to read. Each line is a `name: value` pair, and lines indented under another line belong inside it, like sub-points under a heading in your notes. The short form `{a: 1, b: 2}` puts several pairs on one line. (Inventories may also use the older INI format: a `[group]` heading followed by host names.)

You sort hosts into **groups** such as `web` and `db`, so you can later say "do this on every machine in the web group". In YAML, a group lists its `hosts`, can set `vars` (variables shared by its hosts) and can contain other groups under `children`. Two groups always exist: `all` (every host) and `ungrouped`. A host can be in several groups, such as `web` and `prod`, so you can pick machines by what they do or by which environment they belong to.

Some variables tell Ansible how to connect:

- `ansible_host`: the real address, when the name in the inventory is just a nickname,
- `ansible_user`, `ansible_port`, `ansible_ssh_private_key_file`: the SSH user, port and private key,
- `ansible_connection: local`: manage the control node itself, without SSH.

Ranges save typing: `web[01:10].example.com` means ten hosts, web01 to web10.

As variables pile up, keep them out of the inventory file, in folders next to it: `group_vars/web.yml` for the web group, `host_vars/db1.yml` for one host, `group_vars/all.yml` for everyone.

To see what Ansible sees, run `ansible-inventory -i inventory.yml --graph` (the tree of groups) or `--host web1` (one host's variables).

Every run names the hosts to act on with a **host pattern**: `web` (one group), `web:db` (hosts in either group), `web:&prod` (hosts in both), `all:!staging` (everything except staging). Adding `--limit web1` narrows any run further.
concepts.code:
# inventory.yml: three hosts in two groups, plus a group of groups
all:
  children:
    web:
      hosts:
        web1: {ansible_host: 10.0.1.11}
        web2: {ansible_host: 10.0.1.12}
    db:
      hosts:
        db1: {ansible_host: 10.0.2.21, ansible_user: admin}
    prod:                     # contains both groups above
      children: {web: {}, db: {}}
  vars:                       # applies to every host
    ansible_user: deploy
# ansible-inventory -i inventory.yml --graph
# @all:
#   |--@ungrouped:
#   |--@web:
#   |  |--web1
#   ...
# ansible -i inventory.yml 'prod:!db' --list-hosts    # prod but not db: web1, web2
takeaways: Groups have hosts, vars and children; all and ungrouped always exist
Keep variables in group_vars/ and host_vars/
Host patterns like `web:&prod` and `--limit` pick which hosts a run touches
pitfalls: Piling many variables into the inventory file instead of group_vars/, where they're hard to find and hard to change for one group.

quiz.q: Which pattern targets hosts that are in both the web and prod groups?

concepts.name: Ad-hoc commands and core modules
concepts.summary: Run a single module on many hosts straight from the terminal, and meet the built-in modules you'll use every day.
concepts.why: Ad-hoc commands answer quick questions across many servers, and they teach you the modules that all bigger Ansible work is built from.
concepts.body:
Sometimes you just want one quick thing done on many servers: restart a service, check how long they've been up. An **ad-hoc command** runs a single module on a group of hosts, straight from the terminal:

`ansible <pattern> -i inventory.yml -m <module> -a "<arguments>"`

`<pattern>` is a host pattern, `-m` names the module and `-a` gives its settings as `key=value` pairs. Useful extra options:

- `-b` ("become"): run as root, using sudo,
- `-K`: ask you for the sudo password,
- `-f 20`: work on 20 hosts at the same time (the default is 5),
- `--check`: a **dry run**, which reports what would change without changing anything.

Modules you'll use daily, all in the built-in set `ansible.builtin`:

- `ping`: checks that Ansible can log in to the host and run modules there.
- `command` runs a program; `shell` runs a line through the shell, so pipes and `>` work. Both report "changed" every time, because Ansible can't tell what the command did, so prefer a specific module when one exists.
- `package`, `apt`, `dnf`: install software; `service`: start, stop or restart services.
- `copy`, `template`, `file`, `lineinfile`: put files on the host and edit their contents.
- `user`, `group`: manage accounts.
- `get_url`, `unarchive`: download files and unpack them.
- `setup`: collects information about the host; `debug`: prints a value.

Write module names in full, like `ansible.builtin.copy`. The part before the last dot names the **collection** the module comes from: a bundle of modules published together. This full form is the **fully qualified collection name** (FQCN). Short names like `copy` still work, but full names are unambiguous, and Ansible's checking tools expect them.

`ansible-doc ansible.builtin.lineinfile` shows any module's documentation, with examples, without needing the internet.
concepts.code:
# can Ansible reach every host?
ansible all -i inventory.yml -m ansible.builtin.ping
# how long has each web server been running?
ansible web -i inventory.yml -m ansible.builtin.command -a "uptime"
# install htop as root (-b); does nothing where it's already installed
ansible web -i inventory.yml -b -m ansible.builtin.apt -a "name=htop state=present update_cache=true"
# ask db1 which operating system it runs
ansible db  -i inventory.yml -m ansible.builtin.setup -a "filter=ansible_distribution*"
# db1 | SUCCESS => { "ansible_facts": { "ansible_distribution": "Ubuntu",
#                    "ansible_distribution_version": "24.04", ... } }
# restart nginx, but only on web1
ansible all -i inventory.yml -b -m ansible.builtin.service -a "name=nginx state=restarted" --limit web1
ansible-doc -s ansible.builtin.copy     # short summary of the module's settings
takeaways: ansible <pattern> -m module -a args; -b to run as root
Prefer specific modules over command and shell
Use full module names (FQCNs) and ansible-doc
pitfalls: Using shell for everything, so tasks stop being idempotent and every run reports a change.

quiz.q: Why prefer ansible.builtin.apt over shell: apt-get install -y nginx?
options: apt is idempotent and reports changed only when it installed something
apt works on every operating system
quiz.explain: The module checks what's installed first; the shell command reports a change every time.

concepts.name: Writing your first playbook
concepts.summary: Write plays with hosts, become and tasks, run them with ansible-playbook and read the recap at the end.
concepts.why: Playbooks are Ansible's real unit of work: saved steps you can run again and again with the same result.
concepts.body:
Ad-hoc commands are one-offs. For a setup you want to repeat, you write the steps down in a file: a **playbook**. A playbook is a YAML file holding a list of **plays**. In YAML, lines that start with `- ` are the items of a list. Each play says which hosts to work on and which tasks to run there, in order.

A play has these keys:

- `hosts`: a host pattern,
- `become: true`: run the tasks as root, using sudo,
- `vars`: variables for this play,
- `tasks`: the ordered list of tasks. Each task has a `name`, printed in the output (always write one), and one module with its settings.

In a playbook, module settings are indented YAML lines (`name: nginx`), not the `key=value` strings of ad-hoc commands.

Tasks run **in order**. Each task runs on all the play's hosts, five at a time by default (the `forks` setting), before the next task starts. If a task fails on one host, that host sits out the rest of the play while the others carry on.

Run a playbook with `ansible-playbook -i inventory.yml site.yml`. Handy options:

- `--check --diff`: a dry run that also shows which lines of each file would change,
- `--limit web1`: only these hosts,
- `--start-at-task "Install nginx"`: skip ahead to one task,
- `--syntax-check` and `--list-tasks`: look for mistakes in the file, or list its tasks, without running anything,
- `-v` up to `-vvvv`: print more and more detail when you're tracking down a problem.

At the end, the **PLAY RECAP** counts how each host's tasks went: `ok` (already right), `changed`, `failed`, `unreachable` (Ansible couldn't connect), `skipped` and a few more. Then run the playbook a second time: it should show `changed=0`.
concepts.code:
# site.yml: one play with three tasks - name: Configure web servers hosts: web # the web group from the inventory become: true # run as root tasks: - name: Install nginx ansible.builtin.apt: name: nginx state: present update_cache: true - name: Deploy the home page ansible.builtin.copy: # {{ inventory_hostname }} is replaced by each host's name content: "

Hello from {{ inventory_hostname }}

\n" dest: /var/www/html/index.html mode: "0644" - name: Ensure nginx is running and starts at boot ansible.builtin.service: {name: nginx, state: started, enabled: true} # ansible-playbook -i inventory.yml site.yml # PLAY RECAP: web1 : ok=4 changed=2 unreachable=0 failed=0 skipped=0 ... # (ok=4 includes the automatic first step that gathers host information)
takeaways: A playbook is a list of plays: hosts + tasks
Each task finishes on all hosts before the next starts
PLAY RECAP: aim for changed=0 on the second run
pitfalls: Leaving tasks unnamed, which makes the output hard to follow when something goes wrong.

quiz.q: Task 2 fails on web1 but succeeds on web2. What happens to task 3 by default?
options: The whole play stops on all hosts
quiz.explain: A failed host is removed from the rest of the play; other hosts continue.

concepts.name: Variables, facts and registered results
concepts.summary: Use variables in playbooks, read the facts Ansible gathers about each host, and save a task's result with register.
concepts.why: Real playbooks adapt to each host; variables and facts are how they know what to do.
concepts.body:
As in a bash script, a variable is a name for a value. In Ansible you use one by writing its name inside double curly braces: `"{{ app_port }}"`. Ansible swaps in the value before running the task. This fill-in-the-blanks notation comes from **Jinja2**, the small language Ansible uses for it.

When a value *starts* with `{{`, put quotes around the whole value. Without them, YAML sees the `{` as the start of a `{a: 1}` group of pairs, and the playbook fails to load.

Variables can be set in many places. The common ones: `vars:` in a play, the `group_vars/` and `host_vars/` folders, and `-e key=value` on the `ansible-playbook` command. Those last ones are **extra vars**, and they beat every other source.

**Facts** are variables Ansible discovers about each host as a play starts: its operating system, IP addresses, CPU, memory and mounted disks. Read them through `ansible_facts`, as in `ansible_facts['distribution']` (for example Ubuntu). The square brackets pick one named entry, and you can chain them to dig deeper: `ansible_facts['default_ipv4']['address']`. Gathering facts takes a moment, so add `gather_facts: false` to plays that don't need them.

Some variables always exist: `inventory_hostname` (this host's name in the inventory), `group_names` (its groups), `groups['web']` (every host in the web group) and `hostvars['db1']` (another host's variables and facts).

`register` saves what a task returned, so later tasks can use it. After `register: result`, `result.stdout` is the command's output, `result.rc` its exit code and `result.changed` whether it changed anything. To print a value while you write a playbook, use the `ansible.builtin.debug` module with `msg:` or `var:`.
concepts.code:
- name: Variables and facts demo
  hosts: localhost
  connection: local
  vars:
    app_name: shop
    app_port: 8080
  tasks:
    - name: Show OS facts
      ansible.builtin.debug:
        msg: "{{ app_name }} on {{ ansible_facts['distribution'] }} {{ ansible_facts['distribution_version'] }}"

    - name: Check what listens on the port
      # ss lists the programs waiting for connections on a port
      ansible.builtin.command: "ss -ltn sport = :{{ app_port }}"
      register: listen
      changed_when: false            # it only reads, so never report a change

    - name: Use the registered result
      # | length counts the output lines; line 1 is a header
      ansible.builtin.debug:
        msg: "Port {{ app_port }} busy: {{ listen.stdout_lines | length > 1 }}"
# ansible-playbook vars.yml -e app_port=9090   # extra vars override play vars
takeaways: Quote values that start with {{
Facts live under ansible_facts; turn gathering off when unneeded
register saves a task's result; -e extra vars beat everything
pitfalls: Writing msg: {{ x }} without quotes: YAML reads the braces as the start of a group of pairs and refuses to load the file.

quiz.q: How do you read the IP address Ansible gathered for host db1 from a play running on web1?
quiz.explain: hostvars exposes every host's variables and gathered facts.

concepts.name: Handlers and change notification
concepts.summary: Restart or reload services only when something actually changed, using notify and handlers.
concepts.why: Restarting a service on every run interrupts it for no reason; handlers restart it only when something actually changed.
concepts.body:
Picture nginx, a program that serves websites, with a configuration file you manage with Ansible. When the file changes, the program must reload it to notice. When nothing changed, reloading would only interrupt visitors for no reason. A **handler** solves this: it's a task that runs only when another task **notifies** it *and* that task reported `changed`.

- Write handlers in the play's `handlers:` section, next to `tasks:`.
- A task adds `notify: Reload nginx`, the handler's name.
- Handlers run **once**, at the **end of the play** (after all tasks), however many tasks notified them, in the order they're written in `handlers:`.

Details worth knowing:

- If a later task fails on a host, that host's waiting handlers don't run, so the file may have changed while the service never reloaded. `--force-handlers` (or `force_handlers: true`) runs them anyway.
- `ansible.builtin.meta: flush_handlers` runs waiting handlers right away, for example to restart a service before a later task checks that it answers.
- `listen: "restart web stack"` lets several handlers respond to one shared name.

Where a service supports it, prefer `state: reloaded` (re-read the settings while staying up) over `restarted` (stop, then start). And check a configuration file before installing it: `template` and `copy` have a `validate:` option that runs a checking command, such as `nginx -t -c %s`, on the new file (`%s` stands for it) and refuses to install the file if the check fails.
concepts.code:
- name: Configure nginx
  hosts: web
  become: true
  tasks:
    - name: Install nginx config
      ansible.builtin.template:
        src: nginx.conf.j2
        dest: /etc/nginx/nginx.conf
        validate: nginx -t -c %s        # test the new file before it replaces the old one
      notify: Reload nginx

    - name: Install site certificate
      ansible.builtin.copy: {src: site.pem, dest: /etc/nginx/site.pem, mode: "0600"}
      notify: Reload nginx              # still only one reload

  handlers:
    - name: Reload nginx
      ansible.builtin.service: {name: nginx, state: reloaded}
# first run: both tasks changed -> RUNNING HANDLER [Reload nginx] once
# second run: nothing changed -> handler not run
takeaways: Handlers run only when a notifying task changed something
They run once, at the end of the play
flush_handlers runs them early; check config files before installing them
pitfalls: Expecting a handler to run when a later task failed on that host; use force_handlers if needed.

quiz.q: Three tasks notify the same handler and two of them report changed. How many times does it run?
quiz.explain: Handlers are deduplicated and run once at the end of the play.

concepts.name: ansible.cfg, SSH and privilege escalation
concepts.summary: Configure Ansible with ansible.cfg, tune how it connects over SSH, and use become safely.
concepts.why: Connection problems are the most common first obstacle, and project config makes runs reproducible.
concepts.body:
Ansible reads one configuration file: the first it finds of `ANSIBLE_CONFIG` (an environment variable naming a file), `./ansible.cfg` in the current directory, `~/.ansible.cfg`, then `/etc/ansible/ansible.cfg`. Keep an `ansible.cfg` in your project so everyone gets the same settings. `ansible-config dump --only-changed` shows what differs from the defaults.

Common settings in `[defaults]`: `inventory`, `remote_user` (the SSH user), `forks`, `roles_path`, `host_key_checking`, and `stdout_callback` (how output is printed). In `[ssh_connection]`: `ssh_args` (extra options for ssh) and `pipelining` (a speed-up covered in the performance lesson).

Ansible connects with your normal `ssh` program, so everything in `~/.ssh/config` applies: users, ports, keys, and `ProxyJump` lines that hop through a middle server. Your ssh-agent works too. To track down a connection problem, run `ansible host -m ping -vvvv`, which prints the exact ssh command Ansible used.

Host key checking is on by default. For brand-new hosts, add their keys to `known_hosts` (for example with `ssh-keyscan`) rather than switching checking off for good.

**Privilege escalation** means running a task as a more powerful user, usually root. In Ansible it's `become`: `become: true` uses `sudo` by default, `become_user: postgres` switches to another user, and `become_method` can be `su`, `doas` and others. Use `-K` (`--ask-become-pass`) when sudo needs a password, or store the password encrypted with Ansible Vault (a later lesson). Turn `become` on for the tasks or plays that need it rather than everywhere, so it's clear what runs as root.
concepts.code:
# ansible.cfg (project root)
[defaults]
inventory = inventory.yml
remote_user = deploy
forks = 20
roles_path = roles
stdout_callback = default
callback_result_format = yaml

[ssh_connection]
pipelining = True
ssh_args = -o ControlMaster=auto -o ControlPersist=60s

# ~/.ssh/config is honoured too, e.g.:
#   Host 10.0.*
#     ProxyJump bastion.example.com
# ansible web1 -m ansible.builtin.ping -vvvv   # shows the ssh command used
takeaways: A project ansible.cfg wins over user and system config
Ansible uses your OpenSSH setup: ssh config, agent and ProxyJump just work
become per task or play; -K for sudo passwords
pitfalls: Setting host_key_checking = False for good, losing protection against man-in-the-middle attacks.

quiz.q: You run ansible-playbook from your project directory, which contains ansible.cfg, and you also have ~/.ansible.cfg. Which is used?
quiz.explain: Ansible uses the first file found, and the current directory comes before the home directory.

concepts.name: Jinja2 templates and filters
concepts.summary: Generate configuration files from Jinja2 templates, filling in variables and using loops, if-blocks and filters.
concepts.why: Most server setup comes down to writing the right configuration file for each host.
concepts.body:
Configuration files often differ a little per host: a name here, a port there. A **template** is such a file with blanks left in. The `ansible.builtin.template` module fills the blanks with each host's variables (this is called **rendering**) on the control node, then copies the result to the host. It reports `changed` only if the content differs. Templates usually live in a `templates/` folder and end in `.j2`.

Inside a template you write Jinja2:

- `{{ expression }}` prints a value.
- `{% if %}...{% endif %}` includes text only when a condition is true.
- `{% for x in list %}...{% endfor %}` repeats text once per item.
- `{# comment #}` is a note that doesn't appear in the output.
- `{%-` and `-%}` remove the blank space and line breaks next to a tag, to keep the output tidy.

A **filter** changes a value on its way out, written after a `|`: `{{ name | upper }}` prints the name in capitals. Common ones: `default('x')` (use x if the variable isn't set), `join(', ')` (glue a list into one string), `to_nice_yaml` and `to_json` (write data out as YAML, or as JSON, another common text format for data), `regex_replace` (search and replace with a regular expression), `combine` (merge two sets of `key: value` pairs) and `mandatory` (fail if the variable isn't set).

**Tests** answer yes-or-no questions with `is`: `x is defined`, `result is succeeded`, `ver is version('2.0', '>=')`.

The same Jinja2 works anywhere in a playbook, not only in template files: in task settings, in variable values and in conditions.

Start each generated file with `{{ ansible_managed | comment }}`. It writes a comment saying Ansible manages the file, so nobody edits it by hand.

Because rendering happens on the control node, **lookups** such as `lookup('file', ...)` and `lookup('env', ...)` (read a file, read an environment variable) read the control node's files and environment, not the target host's.
takeaways: template renders on the control node and copies only if changed
Filters (|) transform values; tests (is) check them
Lookups read the control node, not the target
pitfalls: Expecting `lookup('file', '/etc/hostname')` to read the target host's file; it reads the control node's.

quiz.q: Where is a Jinja2 template rendered when you use ansible.builtin.template?
options: On the first host in the group
On the control node, then the result is copied
quiz.explain: Rendering happens on the control node with the host's variables; only the finished file travels to the host.

concepts.name: Conditionals and loops
concepts.summary: Run tasks only when a condition holds with when, and repeat them over lists and key-value data with loop.
concepts.why: One playbook must handle different operating systems, environments, and lists of users, packages or sites.
concepts.body:
`when` makes a task run only on hosts where a condition is true. Write the condition as plain Jinja2, *without* `{{ }}`:

- `when: ansible_facts['os_family'] == "Debian"`
- `when: result.rc != 0`, `when: feature_enabled | bool`
- A list means all must be true: `when: [a, b]`.

Since ansible-core 2.19, a condition must come out as a real **boolean**: exactly true or false. A string such as `"yes"` is not enough, so `when: some_var` with `some_var: "yes"` is an error. Convert it with `| bool`, or compare: `when: some_var == "yes"`.

`loop` repeats a task once for each item in a list. Inside the task, the current item is called `item`:

- `loop: [nginx, git, htop]`
- over a list of entries such as `{name: ana, admin: true}`: use `item.name` and `item.admin`,
- over a set of `key: value` pairs such as `features`: `loop: "{{ features | dict2items }}"` turns each pair into an item with `item.key` and `item.value`.

`loop_control` adjusts the loop: `label: "{{ item.name }}"` prints just the name in the output instead of the whole item, and `pause: 2` waits two seconds between items.

With `loop`, `when` is checked **for each item**, so some items can be skipped. Registering a looped task gives `result.results`: a list with one entry per item.

Many modules accept a whole list at once (`apt: name: [nginx, git]`). That's faster than a loop, because the module runs once instead of once per item.
concepts.code:
- name: Users and packages
  hosts: localhost
  connection: local
  vars:
    users:
      - {name: ana, admin: true}
      - {name: bo, admin: false}
    features: {gzip: "yes", http3: "no"}
  tasks:
    - name: Show admins only
      ansible.builtin.debug:
        msg: "{{ item.name }} is an admin"
      loop: "{{ users }}"
      loop_control: {label: "{{ item.name }}"}
      when: item.admin

    - name: Enabled features
      ansible.builtin.debug:
        msg: "feature {{ item.key }} on"
      loop: "{{ features | dict2items }}"
      when: item.value | bool          # explicit boolean conversion
# ok: [localhost] => (item=ana) => msg: ana is an admin
# skipping: [localhost] => (item=bo)
takeaways: when is plain Jinja2 and must give a real true or false
loop with item; dict2items for key-value data; loop_control label
Pass lists directly to modules that accept them
pitfalls: Wrapping when conditions in {{ }}, which triggers warnings and can break them.

quiz.q: Why write when: item.value | bool for values like "yes" and "no"?
options: A string like "no" isn't a true or false value, so ansible-core rejects it; | bool converts it
It renders the value on the target
quiz.explain: | bool turns 'yes' and 'no' into true and false, and modern ansible-core requires a real boolean.

concepts.name: Roles and project layout
concepts.summary: Pack tasks, handlers, templates, files and default settings into reusable roles, and build playbooks from them.
concepts.why: Roles are how Ansible code stays organised and reusable beyond a single playbook.
concepts.body:
As playbooks grow, you'll want to reuse your "set up nginx" steps in other playbooks and projects. A **role** packs everything for one job (tasks, handlers, templates, files and default settings) into a folder with a fixed layout that Ansible knows how to load:

- `tasks/main.yml`: where the role's tasks start,
- `handlers/main.yml`, `templates/`, `files/`: found automatically, no paths needed,
- `defaults/main.yml`: default values for the role's variables,
- `vars/main.yml`: the role's own internal values,
- `meta/main.yml`: information about the role, such as other roles it needs.

The difference between `defaults` and `vars` matters. Defaults have the **lowest priority** of any variable, so whoever uses the role can replace them from the inventory or the play: they are the role's knobs. Values in `vars/` have high priority and aren't meant to be changed by users.

`ansible-galaxy role init roles/nginx` creates the folders for you.

Using roles:

- `roles:` in a play runs the listed roles before the play's own `tasks`.
- Inside tasks, `ansible.builtin.import_role` is read when the playbook loads, before anything runs, so it's fixed. `include_role` is read only when the run reaches it, so it can be combined with `loop` or `when`.
- The same pair exists for plain task files: `import_tasks` and `include_tasks`.

Design tips: one role per piece of software (`nginx`, `app`); start variable names with the role name (`nginx_worker_processes`) so two roles never clash; give every variable a sensible default; never write fixed host names into a role. Keep values specific to your servers in the inventory's `group_vars`.

A typical project holds `ansible.cfg`, an `inventory/` folder (with `group_vars`), a `site.yml` that pulls in one playbook per kind of server (`webservers.yml`), a `roles/` folder, and `requirements.yml` listing roles and collections from elsewhere (a later lesson).
concepts.code:
# roles/nginx/defaults/main.yml
nginx_worker_processes: auto
nginx_sites: []

# roles/nginx/tasks/main.yml
- name: Install nginx
  ansible.builtin.package: {name: nginx, state: present}
- name: Configure nginx
  ansible.builtin.template: {src: nginx.conf.j2, dest: /etc/nginx/nginx.conf}
  notify: Reload nginx

# roles/nginx/handlers/main.yml
- name: Reload nginx
  ansible.builtin.service: {name: nginx, state: reloaded}

# webservers.yml
- name: Web tier
  hosts: web
  become: true
  roles:
    - role: nginx
      vars: {nginx_worker_processes: 4}
takeaways: Fixed layout: tasks, handlers, templates, files, defaults, vars, meta
defaults = knobs users may change; vars = internal
import_* is fixed when loaded, include_* is decided while running
pitfalls: Putting settings users should tune in vars/main.yml, where inventory variables can't replace them.

quiz.q: Where should a role put values that users are expected to change from group_vars?
quiz.explain: Role defaults have the lowest priority, so any inventory or play variable replaces them.

concepts.name: Secrets with Ansible Vault
concepts.summary: Encrypt passwords and other secrets with ansible-vault so they can be stored safely alongside your playbooks.
concepts.why: Playbooks need passwords and keys; saving them as readable text in your project leaks them to anyone who sees the files.
concepts.body:
Playbooks often need **secrets**: passwords, private keys, access codes for other services. Ansible projects are usually kept in git, a tool that records every version of a project's files and shares them with your team. Anything written there in readable form can be read by everyone with access, in every old version, for good.

**Ansible Vault** encrypts such data with a password you give when you run the playbook. Encrypted data looks like a block of random characters; Ansible decrypts it only while it runs, without saving a readable copy.

Two ways to use it:

- **Encrypted files**: `ansible-vault create group_vars/prod/vault.yml`, or `encrypt` an existing file. The whole file is stored encrypted; `ansible-vault edit` opens it decrypted in your editor for a moment, and `view` shows it.
- **Encrypted strings**: `ansible-vault encrypt_string 's3cr3t' --name db_password` prints a `!vault |` block you paste into an otherwise readable variables file.

A common habit: in `group_vars/prod/`, keep a readable `vars.yml` with `db_password: "{{ vault_db_password }}"`, and an encrypted `vault.yml` with `vault_db_password: ...`. You can still search for every variable name, while the values stay encrypted.

Giving the password: `--ask-vault-pass` (type it in), or `--vault-password-file` pointing to a file that holds it, or to a script that fetches it from a password store (the usual choice on automated build servers). **Vault IDs** (`--vault-id prod@prompt`) let each environment have its own password.

Add `no_log: true` to tasks that handle secrets, so their values never appear in the output or in logs.

Vault protects secrets stored in your files. Anyone with the vault password, or with root on a server the secret is sent to, can still read them. Larger teams often keep secrets in a **secrets manager** instead: a locked-down service such as HashiCorp Vault or AWS Secrets Manager that hands out secrets only to those allowed. Ansible can look values up there while it runs.
concepts.code:
ansible-vault create group_vars/prod/vault.yml      # opens $EDITOR, saves encrypted
ansible-vault encrypt_string 'S3cr3t!' --name vault_db_password
# vault_db_password: !vault |
#           $ANSIBLE_VAULT;1.1;AES256
#           6231363436643837...

cat group_vars/prod/vars.yml
# db_password: "{{ vault_db_password }}"     # readable indirection

ansible-playbook -i inventory.yml site.yml --vault-password-file ~/.vault-pass.sh
ansible-vault rekey group_vars/prod/vault.yml          # rotate the vault password
takeaways: Encrypt whole files or single strings; edit with ansible-vault edit
vars.yml points to vault_ variables in vault.yml
no_log: true on tasks handling secrets
pitfalls: Printing secrets with the `debug` module, or letting a failing task show them, without no_log: they end up in logs others can read.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of keeping db_password: "{{ vault_db_password }}" in an unencrypted vars file?
options: It avoids needing a vault password
Variable names stay searchable while values stay encrypted
quiz.explain: The readable file shows which variables exist and lets you search for them, without exposing the secret values.

concepts.name: Variable precedence and scoping
concepts.summary: Know which of Ansible's many variable sources wins, and organise variables so the answer is obvious.
concepts.why: "Why isn't this variable the value I set?" is the most common Ansible puzzle.
concepts.body:
Ansible combines variables from over twenty places. When the same name is set in two of them, the one with higher **precedence** (priority) wins. You don't need the whole list, just the landmarks, from lowest to highest:

1. role `defaults/`
2. inventory variables: group vars (`all`, then parent groups, then child groups), then host vars; files in `group_vars/`/`host_vars/` beat variables written inside the inventory file
3. facts, including facts saved from earlier runs
4. play `vars`, `vars_prompt`, `vars_files`
5. role `vars/` and `include_vars`
6. block and task `vars`
7. `set_fact` and `register`
8. role parameters (values given where a role is used, like `vars:` under `- role: nginx`) and `include_role` parameters
9. **extra vars** (`-e`), which always win.

Group order: when a host is in two sibling groups (neither inside the other), the group whose name sorts **later alphabetically** wins, unless you set `ansible_group_priority`. Relying on that is fragile; avoid setting the same variable in sibling groups.

A variable can hold a whole set of `key: value` pairs, a **dictionary**. Dictionaries are **replaced**, not merged, by default: a host-level `nginx: {port: 81}` wipes out the group-level `nginx: {port: 80, workers: 4}`, and `workers` is gone. Prefer flat variables with a prefix (`nginx_port`), or merge on purpose with the `combine` filter.

Practical rules: defaults in role `defaults`, environment and group values in `group_vars`, the odd host that differs in `host_vars`, and `-e` only for one-off changes. To see the result, run `ansible-inventory --host web1` or a `debug: var=...` task.
concepts.code:
# roles/app/defaults/main.yml
app_port: 8080
app_settings: {workers: 4, log_level: info}

# inventory/group_vars/prod.yml
app_port: 80
app_settings: {log_level: warn}       # replaces the whole dict: workers is gone

# better: merge explicitly in the role
#   app_effective: "{{ app_settings_default | combine(app_settings_override | default({})) }}"

# ansible-inventory -i inventory --host web1 | grep -A3 app_
# ansible-playbook site.yml -e app_port=9000   # extra vars beat everything
takeaways: Role defaults lowest, extra vars highest; host vars beat group vars
Sibling groups: later alphabetical wins unless ansible_group_priority
Dicts are replaced, not merged; prefer flat vars or combine
pitfalls: Setting one key of a dictionary variable at host level and silently losing all its other keys.

quiz.q: A variable is set in role defaults, group_vars/all and host_vars/web1. Which value does web1 get?
quiz.explain: Host variables beat group variables, which beat role defaults.

concepts.name: Error handling, blocks and changed_when
concepts.summary: Define what counts as failure and change, group tasks in blocks, and recover with rescue and always.
concepts.why: Real automation must cope with expected non-zero exit codes and partial failures without lying about state.
concepts.body:
By default a task fails when its module says so; for `command` and `shell`, that means a non-zero exit code. You can redefine both "failed" and "changed":

- `failed_when: result.rc not in [0, 2]`, or `"'ERROR' in result.stderr"` (the error output mentions ERROR).
- `changed_when: false` for commands that only read; `changed_when: "'created' in result.stdout"` for commands that sometimes change things. Truthful change reports keep handlers and the recap honest.
- `ignore_errors: true` carries on after a failure (use it sparingly; it hides problems). `ignore_unreachable: true` carries on when a host can't be reached.

A **block** groups tasks so they share settings such as `when` and `become`, and it adds a way to recover from failure:

- `block:` the main tasks,
- `rescue:` runs if any task in the block fails; if the rescue tasks succeed, the host counts as recovered (`rescued=1` in the recap) and carries on,
- `always:` runs either way, for cleanup or a final note.

If you know another programming language, this is try, catch and finally.

Controlling how far a failure spreads across hosts:

- `any_errors_fatal: true` stops the play on all hosts as soon as one fails. Use it for a **cluster**: several servers working together as one system, which must stay in step.
- `max_fail_percentage: 20` stops once too many hosts have failed.
- `serial: 2` (or `"25%"`) runs the whole play on a few hosts at a time before moving to the next few. This is a **rolling update**: if one round fails, the rollout stops before it reaches every host.

`retries`, `delay` and `until` repeat a task until a condition holds. That's ideal for waiting until a freshly started app passes its **health check**: a simple "are you OK?" web address that answers status 200 when the app is ready.
concepts.code:
- name: Rolling deploy
  hosts: app
  serial: "25%"
  max_fail_percentage: 0
  tasks:
    - name: Deploy with rollback
      block:
        # 'current' is a symbolic link (a shortcut); point it at the new release folder
        - name: Switch symlink to the new release
          ansible.builtin.file: {src: "/opt/app/{{ release }}", dest: /opt/app/current, state: link}
        # ask the app's health address every 3 s, up to 10 times
        - name: Wait for health check
          ansible.builtin.uri: {url: "http://localhost:8080/healthz", status_code: 200}
          register: health
          retries: 10
          delay: 3
          until: health is succeeded
      rescue:
        - name: Roll back to previous release
          ansible.builtin.file: {src: "/opt/app/{{ previous_release }}", dest: /opt/app/current, state: link}
        - name: Mark host failed after rollback
          ansible.builtin.fail: {msg: "Release {{ release }} failed health checks"}
      always:
        - name: Record the attempt
          ansible.builtin.lineinfile: {path: /var/log/deploys.log, line: "{{ release }} {{ health.status | default('n/a') }}", create: true}
takeaways: failed_when and changed_when make results truthful
block, rescue, always: try, recover, clean up
serial + max_fail_percentage give safe rolling updates; until and retries wait for health
pitfalls: Using ignore_errors: true to make a playbook green, hiding real failures.

quiz.q: A task inside block fails and its rescue section succeeds. How does the host end up?
options: Skipped for the rest of the play
quiz.explain: A successful rescue clears the failure, so the host continues with the play.

concepts.name: Collections and Galaxy
concepts.summary: Install and pin collections and roles with requirements.yml, and understand how content is namespaced.
concepts.why: Most modules (for cloud providers, network devices and other software) ship in collections, not in ansible-core itself.
concepts.body:
Since Ansible 2.10, modules, roles and **plugins** (add-ons that run on the control node, such as Jinja2 filters) ship in collections that you install separately. Each collection has a two-part name: a **namespace**, the publisher, like a family name, then the collection's own name: `community.general`, `amazon.aws`, `ansible.posix`.

`ansible-core` includes only `ansible.builtin`; the bigger `ansible` package adds a hand-picked set of collections on top. That's why full module names matter: `community.postgresql.postgresql_db` tells readers and Ansible exactly where a module comes from.

Collections are installed from **Ansible Galaxy** (galaxy.ansible.com, the public sharing site), from Red Hat's Automation Hub, from a private Galaxy server or from a git repository:

- `ansible-galaxy collection install community.general`
- for a project, list everything in `requirements.yml` with allowed versions and install it all with `ansible-galaxy install -r requirements.yml` (this handles roles and collections).

Collections install to `~/.ansible/collections` by default. Set `collections_path` (or install with `-p ./collections`) to keep a project's collections inside the project, so automated runs on a build server get exactly the same versions every time.

`ansible-galaxy collection list` shows what is installed, and where. Watch for duplicates: the same collection in two places, where the first one found wins.

Some collections also need Python **libraries** (ready-made code other programs use) on the control node or the target: `boto3` for `amazon.aws`, `kubernetes` for `kubernetes.core`.

For a fully repeatable setup, Red Hat's **execution environments** bundle ansible-core, your collections and their libraries into one **container image**: a packaged, ready-to-run copy of software that behaves the same on every machine. You build one with `ansible-builder`.
concepts.code:
# requirements.yml
collections:
  - name: community.general
    version: ">=10.0.0,<11.0.0"
  - name: ansible.posix
    version: ">=2.0.0"
  - name: kubernetes.core
    version: "6.1.0"
roles:
  - name: geerlingguy.docker
    version: "7.4.1"
# ansible-galaxy install -r requirements.yml -p ./collections   (roles: use roles_path)
# ansible-galaxy collection list | grep -E 'community.general|kubernetes.core'
# usage in a task:
#   - community.general.timezone: {name: Europe/Berlin}
takeaways: ansible-core has only ansible.builtin; everything else is in collections
Pin collections and roles in requirements.yml
Install into the project for repeatable runs; execution environments for full isolation
pitfalls: Relying on whatever collection versions happen to be on a laptop instead of a pinned requirements.yml.

quiz.q: A playbook using community.general.ufw fails with 'couldn't resolve module' on a fresh ansible-core install. Why?
options: The community.general collection isn't installed with ansible-core
quiz.explain: ansible-core ships only ansible.builtin; install the collection from Galaxy.

concepts.name: Check mode, linting and Molecule
concepts.summary: Preview changes with --check --diff, enforce best practices with ansible-lint, and test roles with Molecule.
concepts.why: Untested automation tends to fail at the worst moment: on the real servers your users depend on.
concepts.body:
**Check mode** (`--check`) asks every module to report what it would change without changing it, and `--diff` shows how files and templates would differ. Together they're a safe preview before a real run. Limits: `command` and `shell` tasks are skipped in check mode (Ansible can't know what they'd do), and tasks that depend on earlier changes may fail. Per task, `check_mode: false` makes a read-only command run even in check mode, and `check_mode: true` makes a task always just pretend.

**ansible-lint** reads your playbooks and roles without running them and flags problems: tasks without names, short module names, `command` used where a module exists, a missing `changed_when`, risky file permissions, and old syntax that is **deprecated** (still works, but will be removed). Profiles from `min` to `production` set how strict it is. Run it automatically whenever someone changes the code; `yamllint` adds checks of YAML formatting.

**Molecule** tests a role from start to finish on throwaway machines. It first creates test machines: usually **containers** (sealed-off boxes on one computer, each acting like a small separate Linux system) or **virtual machines** (whole pretend computers running inside a real one). Then it applies the role; Molecule calls this step `converge`.

Next it applies the role a second time to prove it's idempotent: any change on the second run fails the test. Then it runs your checks, such as Ansible `assert` tasks, which fail when a condition is false, and finally deletes the test machines. `molecule test` runs the whole sequence; `molecule converge` and `molecule login` help while you develop.

A good automated pipeline runs yamllint, ansible-lint, `--syntax-check`, Molecule for each role on every OS version you support, and a `--check --diff` run against a test copy of your servers (staging) before the real ones.
concepts.code:
ansible-playbook -i inventory/prod site.yml --check --diff --limit web1
# TASK [nginx : Configure nginx]
# --- before: /etc/nginx/nginx.conf
# +++ after: /etc/nginx/nginx.conf
# -worker_processes 2;
# +worker_processes 4;
# changed: [web1]

ansible-lint --profile production roles/nginx
# name[missing]: All tasks should be named. roles/nginx/tasks/main.yml:12
# fqcn[action-core]: Use FQCN for builtin module actions (service).

cd roles/nginx && molecule test
# ... converge, idempotence: "Idempotence completed successfully.", verify, destroy
takeaways: --check --diff previews changes; commands are skipped in check mode
ansible-lint flags bad habits automatically
Molecule creates test machines, applies the role twice, checks and deletes
pitfalls: Trusting check mode for playbooks full of shell tasks, which it simply skips.

quiz.q: What does Molecule's idempotence step check?
options: That the role runs faster the second time
That the role works on every OS
That a second converge reports no changes
quiz.explain: A second run that changes anything means the role isn't idempotent, and the test fails.

concepts.name: Performance: forks, pipelining, async
concepts.summary: Speed up large runs with more forks, SSH connection reuse, pipelining, saved facts, the free strategy and background (async) tasks.
concepts.why: A playbook that takes an hour on 500 hosts can often take minutes with the right settings.
concepts.body:
Where the time goes: for each task and host, Ansible opens an SSH session, makes a temporary folder, copies the module there, runs it and cleans up. Each setting below cuts one of those costs:

- **forks** (default 5): how many hosts work on a task at the same time. Raise it to 25-100 for big fleets; the control node's CPU and memory set the limit.
- **SSH multiplexing**: `ControlMaster`/`ControlPersist` (on by default in Ansible's ssh options) keeps one SSH connection, logged in once, open and reuses it for many tasks.
- **pipelining** (`pipelining = True`): sends the module through the open session's standard input instead of copying it as a file first, saving several SSH steps per task. It needs sudo on the hosts not to insist on a terminal (the `requiretty` setting).
- **Facts**: `gather_facts: false` when you don't need them, `gather_subset` to collect fewer, or **fact caching**: save facts to files (`jsonfile`) or a fast in-memory store (`redis`) and, with `gathering = smart`, reuse them on later runs instead of collecting them again.
- **Strategies**: the default `linear` waits for all hosts at each task; `free` lets each host race ahead on its own. `serial` rounds trade speed for safety.
- **async**: `async: 600, poll: 0` starts a long task (a big download, a backup) in the background, so Ansible doesn't wait for it, and moves on; check on it later with `async_status`.
- Fewer tasks: pass lists to package modules instead of looping, and write one `template` rather than many `lineinfile` edits.

Measure before tuning: the `profile_tasks` and `timer` callback plugins (plugins that react to events during a run) print how long each task and the whole run took. Turn them on with `callbacks_enabled = ansible.posix.profile_tasks, ansible.posix.timer`.
concepts.code:
# ansible.cfg
[defaults]
forks = 50
gathering = smart
fact_caching = jsonfile
fact_caching_connection = .facts_cache
fact_caching_timeout = 86400
callbacks_enabled = ansible.posix.profile_tasks, ansible.posix.timer

[ssh_connection]
pipelining = True
ssh_args = -o ControlMaster=auto -o ControlPersist=300s

# playbook snippet:
#   - hosts: all
#     strategy: free
#     gather_facts: false
#     tasks:
#       - ansible.builtin.command: /usr/local/bin/backup.sh
#         async: 3600
#         poll: 0
#         register: backup_job
takeaways: Raise forks; keep SSH multiplexing; turn on pipelining
Skip, trim or cache facts
free strategy and async for independent or long tasks; profile_tasks to measure
pitfalls: Turning on pipelining for hosts where sudo is set to require a terminal (requiretty), so become tasks fail.

options: Copying module files to the host as separate SSH operations for each task
quiz.explain: With pipelining, modules are streamed through the existing SSH session instead of copied and then executed.

concepts.name: Dynamic inventory plugins
concepts.summary: Build the host list at run time from cloud providers and other sources with inventory plugins, and shape groups with keyed_groups and constructed.
concepts.why: In a cloud, servers come and go all the time; a hand-written host list is always out of date.
concepts.body:
An **inventory plugin** builds the host list at the start of each run by asking an outside source which machines exist right now, usually through a cloud provider's **API** (the set of requests a service accepts from programs). You configure it with a YAML file whose name ends the way the plugin expects (for example `*.aws_ec2.yml`) and whose `plugin:` key names it:

- `amazon.aws.aws_ec2` (Amazon's cloud servers), `azure.azcollection.azure_rm`, `google.cloud.gcp_compute`,
- `kubernetes.core.k8s`, `community.vmware.vmware_vm_inventory`, `netbox.netbox.nb_inventory`.

Common options:

- `filters`: which machines to include (running ones, tagged `env: prod`).
- `keyed_groups`: make groups from a machine's details, such as one group per value of its `role` tag, so plays can target `role_web`.
- `groups`: groups from Jinja2 conditions.
- `compose`: set host variables from those details (`ansible_host: private_ip_address`).
- `hostnames`: what to call each host.
- `cache: true`: remember the answer for a while instead of asking the API on every run.

The **constructed** plugin applies the same `keyed_groups`/`groups`/`compose` logic on top of any other inventory source. You can also point `-i` at a folder that mixes plain inventory files and plugin files; Ansible merges them in alphabetical order.

If you restrict which plugins may run, enable yours with `enable_plugins` in the `[inventory]` section. Test with `ansible-inventory -i inventory/ --graph`.

Old-style inventory scripts (programs that print the host list as JSON) still work, but plugins are the supported way.
concepts.code:
# inventory/prod.aws_ec2.yml
plugin: amazon.aws.aws_ec2
regions: [eu-west-1]
filters:
  instance-state-name: running
  "tag:env": prod
hostnames: [tag:Name]
keyed_groups:
  - key: tags.role
    prefix: role
compose:
  ansible_host: private_ip_address
cache: true
cache_plugin: ansible.builtin.jsonfile
cache_connection: .inventory_cache
# ansible-inventory -i inventory/ --graph
# @all:
#   |--@aws_ec2:
#   |--@role_web:
#   |  |--web-prod-1
takeaways: Inventory plugins ask the source at run time: no out-of-date host lists
keyed_groups, groups and compose shape groups and variables
constructed adds the same logic to any source; cache saves API calls
pitfalls: Naming the config file without the plugin's required suffix, so Ansible doesn't recognise it.

quiz.q: How do you target all EC2 instances tagged role=web with the aws_ec2 plugin configuration above?
options: hosts: tag_role_web only via a script
quiz.explain: keyed_groups with prefix role creates the group role_web from the tag value.

concepts.name: How tasks execute: modules, plugins, templating
concepts.summary: Follow a task from parsing to AnsiballZ on the target, distinguish modules from plugins, and know the 2.19+ templating rules.
concepts.why: Writing modules, debugging odd behaviour and upgrading ansible-core all need this model.
concepts.body:
On the **control node**, Ansible first reads the playbook and works out its structure (it **parses** it), then builds the host list. For each task and host, a worker process (one per fork) prepares the task: it fills in the task's settings with that host's variables, then hands it to an **action plugin**. Most modules use the plain `normal` action; some (`template`, `copy`, `fetch`) have action plugins that do work on the control node first, such as rendering the template locally.

The **connection plugin** (`ssh`, `local`, `paramiko`, `winrm` for Windows, `kubectl` for Kubernetes...) carries code and data to the host. A Python module is bundled with the shared helper code it uses (`module_utils`) into one self-unpacking file called **AnsiballZ**. That file is sent to the target and run with the target's Python, and it answers with a small report in **JSON**, a common text format for data (`changed`, `failed`, `msg`, plus results). Set `ANSIBLE_KEEP_REMOTE_FILES=1` to leave the file on the host so you can inspect it.

So: **modules** run on targets; **plugins** (lookup, filter, callback, inventory, connection, become, cache, strategy) run on the control node.

Writing a module: a Python file that uses `AnsibleModule`, declares the settings it accepts in an `argument_spec`, supports check mode, and reports `changed` truthfully. Put it in a collection's `plugins/modules/` folder (or a role's `library/`).

ansible-core 2.19 reworked templating with **data tagging**: every value remembers where it came from and whether it can be trusted, so error messages point to the exact file and line. Stricter rules came with it: conditions must be booleans, Jinja2 found inside untrusted data (such as a command's output) is no longer evaluated, and some forgiving old behaviour is gone. Read the porting guides (upgrade notes) before moving from 2.18 to 2.19 or later.
concepts.code:
#!/usr/bin/python
# library/greeting_file.py: a minimal idempotent module
from pathlib import Path
from ansible.module_utils.basic import AnsibleModule

def main():
    module = AnsibleModule(
        argument_spec={"path": {"type": "path", "required": True},
                       "name": {"type": "str", "default": "world"}},
        supports_check_mode=True)
    path, text = Path(module.params["path"]), f"hello {module.params['name']}\n"
    changed = not path.exists() or path.read_text() != text
    if changed and not module.check_mode:
        path.write_text(text)
    module.exit_json(changed=changed, path=str(path))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
# - greeting_file: {path: /tmp/greet.txt, name: ana}   -> changed, then ok
takeaways: Templating and action plugins run on the controller; modules run on targets
Python modules travel as AnsiballZ payloads and return JSON
2.19+ data tagging: stricter, better-located templating errors
pitfalls: Writing a custom module that always returns changed=True, breaking handlers and idempotence checks.

quiz.q: Where does a filter plugin like to_nice_yaml run?
options: On the control node during templating
quiz.explain: All plugins, including filters, run on the controller; only modules run on targets.
